newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore brokers suffer as share trading dwindles.
newsitem.headline: Singapore brokers suffer as share trading dwindles.

text.p: Singapore stockbrokers appear to be heading for another bad year as investors avoid the island in favour of other Asian markets, dealers and analysts said on Thursday.

"From the broker's perspective, the first half of the year wasn't so bad, but since June turnover has been pretty pathetic," said Mano Sabnani, head of research of the securities arm of the Development Bank of Singapore Ltd.

During the first eight months of 1996, turnover of Singapore dollar-denominated and Malaysian over-the-counter shares on the Stock Exchange of Singapore fell by 8.9 percent to 21.4 billion shares from 23.5 billion a year earlier, according to figures published by the Straits Times newspaper.

After a spectacularly good January, which saw 6.3 billion shares traded against 2.2 billion in January 1995, volumes in the past three months have crashed to around half the total during the same period last year.
In August, only 1.7 billion shares were traded, 55.3 percent below the year-earlier figure.

Dealers say the high turnover in January was due to the bull market at the end of 1995 which pushed the benchmark Straits Times Industrials Index (STII) of shares up more than 20 percent to a high of just over 2,500 points on February 6.
But since then the index has lost almost all those gains. It closed on Wednesday at 2,094.48 points.

Many foreign institutions and fund buyers now say they prefer to invest in the buoyant Tokyo or Hong Kong markets or in some of the more volatile emerging Southeast Asian markets such as Manila which can offer spectacular capital gains.
Analysts say Singapore's large banks are unlikely to suffer badly from the downturn in traded volumes.

Stockbroking accounted for only 1.8 percent DBS's total earnings in 1995. Overseas Union Bank Ltd, which had the biggest contribution from broking of the local banks, still only earned 5.3 percent of its total revenue from share dealing.
But Singapore's smaller stockbroking companies, such as Vickers Ballas and Kay Hian James Capel (KHJC), may be hit hard, analysts say.

Net profits for both companies fell in 1995. Vickers' 1995 net dipped 4.7 percent to S$34.41 million last year while KHJC's net tumbled 29.8 percent to S$42.62 million. Both firms are due to report first-half 1996 results this month.

"Looking at the first half of the year, my guess is net profits will be up a little. But the second half looks like a killer. I think 1996 as a whole will be worse again than 1995," said one stock analyst, who declined to be identified.

Chen Young Mee, deputy director of Vickers Investment Research, said it was clear from the accounts of Singapore banks, which reported their first-half results in August, that revenue from broking was up slightly in the first-half of 1996.
"But second-half, the volume has been very low. If this continues, it cannot be good for stockbrokers," she said.
Sabnani said the prospects for brokerages could turn around quickly if the local market had something to trade on.
"Once you get an uptrend or a clear downtrend, the volume will come in... But right now, with a long period of consolidation, it is very bad for stockbroking," he said.
Lim Eng Hai, head of research at brokerage J.M. Sassoon, said a couple of really good months could reverse the 1996 full-year results for broking firms.
"1996 has been schizophrenic so far," he said. "But stockbrokers are always hoping for better news (or worse news) just around the corner."
